en: The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-karmavastu on Leather,
Volume One,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in the village of Vatsaka, there was an elder named Balasena, whose wealth was like that of King Vaiśravaṇa. Having been married for a long time, he had no children at all, which gave rise to a sorrowful thought:
"I am now very wealthy and possess much precious property, yet I have no offspring. Should I die one day, because I have no heir, my wealth and goods will be confiscated by the state."
His relatives, acquaintances, and friends, having heard of this, all came to console him, asking:
"For what reason do you remain thus in such sorrow and distress? He replied:
"I have no sons or daughters; I fear that after my death my property will be confiscated by the government, and for this reason I am anxious.
His relatives replied, "You should pray to the gods and spirits; you shall surely obtain sons and daughters."
He then replied, "If it be so, I shall make a request.

For the sake of obtaining a son, he immediately prayed to Maheśvara, the deities of the four great oceans, Vaiśravaṇa, Śakra, and Brahmā; he made requests to all such celestial deities to grant him a son or daughter. He sought them from all the deities of the gardens, the deities of the wilderness, the deities of the crossroads, the deities who receive offerings, the co-nascent deities, the deities of common dharma, and the ever-attendant deities; he sought them from them all.
When the people saw that she had still not obtained a son or daughter despite her prayers to the various deities, they all said:

"If one could obtain a son or daughter by petitioning the heavenly gods, then everyone in the world who sought them would surely obtain them, and there would be no difference between them and a Wheel-Turning King who possesses a full thousand sons."
"However, it is only through the presence of three conditions that a male or female comes into being. What are these three?

The parents must have a mind of desire and come together; the mother’s menstrual period must have arrived; and an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) must be present. Only when all these conditions are met does a child come to exist."
Nevertheless, that householder prayed without ceasing for the sake of obtaining a son or daughter.
Later, at another time, a certain being (sattva) whose life had ended elsewhere came to take conception in the womb of the householder’s wife.
An intelligent woman is skilled in knowing five things. What are these five?
First, she knows whether a man has a mind of passion or a mind free from passion.
2. Knowing the proper time and season;
3. Knowing that she has conceived;
4. Knowing from which man she has conceived.
5. He knows whether it is male or female; if it is male, the fetus is on the right side, and if female, it is on the left side.
Once the elder’s wife had conceived, she was filled with great joy and said to her husband:
"O noble one!..."
"O Benevolent One, do you know now?
I already have a son; he is currently on my right side, so you may be certain it will be a boy.
Upon hearing this, the elder was filled with great joy; he raised his right hand, looked upward and smiled, speaking these words:
"For a long time, I have prayed to the heavenly deities, seeking sons and daughters to assist with the affairs of my household and relieve me of my labors.
What I am unable to accomplish, they shall do for me; thus may our lineage flourish and endure for a long time."
"If I should die after this, you must perform merit on my behalf by reciting my name, and you should wish that my father be reborn in a good realm.

Once he knew he had a son, he immediately had him placed upon a high tower to play as he pleased; he provided fire during the cold and sought coolness during the heat, ensuring he ate at the proper times and was given whatever food was suitable for him.
Regarding the six periods of the day, she proceeds in accordance with the time, all in full conformity with the Dharma.

Adorned with necklaces and ornaments, she is just like a celestial maiden wandering in the Joyful Garden; from couch to couch and from footstool to footstool, her feet do not touch the ground, nor does she allow herself to hear any unpleasant sounds.
When ten months had been fulfilled and the time for birth drew near, he was born under the constellation Śravaṇā.
His son was handsome and pleasing to behold; upon his ears were jeweled earrings, and pearls emerged from them spontaneously.
The father said to his attendants,
"You may summon those who are experts in appraising jewels.
Once they had been summoned, he addressed them, saying:
"How much is the value of this jewel?
He replied, "No one is able to place a price upon it."
"By established custom, priceless jewels are all valued at one *koṭi* of gold coins.
At that time, seventy days had passed since the son’s birth; he gathered his kinsmen and conferred upon him a name.
At that time, his relatives consulted one another, saying:
"What name shall we give him?
The relatives spoke together:
"This one was born under the constellation Śravaṇā; furthermore, her ears are adorned with precious jeweled earrings, each jewel being worth ten million [krores].
It is for this reason."
"The child may be named Wén Jùzhī ěr (Hearing Ten Million Ears).
On the day of his birth, within the house of the elder, two sons were born to a maidservant; the first was named Nú (Slave) and the second was named Yǒnghù (Protector).
The elder immediately ordered that he be nursed and entrusted him to eight nurses to care for him:
two to constantly hold him in their arms, two to provide him with milk and food, two to bathe him, and two to constantly play and amuse him.

These eight nurses attended him day and night, constantly providing milk, curd, butter, and the finest clarified butter (*ghṛta*), along with other exquisite and delicious foods; thus, like a lotus in water, he grew rapidly.

Once he had grown up, he was taught the arts; first he studied writing and arithmetic, as well as the valuation of goods, the distinction between types of clothing and wood, the distinction between various jewels and elephants, and the distinction between men and women—these eight categories he mastered completely.
His father then had three types of chambers constructed for him— namely, for winter, summer, and autumn—
and further created three types of gardens and three types of palaces, distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went together with his court ladies to the upper pavilion to sport and play.
As for the householder Balasena, he performed all the domestic affairs himself, including the plowing and cultivation of the fields.
Seeing his father personally engaged in agricultural labor— plowing and tilling— the son said to his father,
"Why do you personally perform such manual work? The elder replied:
“I shall go as well; like you, I have enjoyed myself playing upon the upper terrace, but that pleasure will soon come to an end.
The son said to his father, “If it is so, please grant me permission: I should enter the sea to gather treasures.”
The father said, "As for the sesame, rice, and five grains that people eat, I can provide you with the same amount of jewels.
My wealth is never lacking; why must you go to sea?"
The son then made his request three times, again saying to his father,
“I pray you grant me permission to go forth to sea.
His father did not comply with his request, so the son spoke to him once more:
“Grant me permission to enter the sea.
Knowing that his son’s resolve was firm and unshakable, the father immediately released him to go.
At that time, the elder rang a bell within the village and made this proclamation:
"Listen, all you who dwell here: my son now wishes to enter the sea to gather treasures.
If there is anyone who would go with him, there shall be no customs duties on the road, nor shall they pay carriage fees or corvée taxes; they must provide their own provisions."
At that time, there were five hundred merchants, each having prepared rice and grain.
Then the elder Brahmadatta invited the five hundred merchants; after providing them with a meal at his home, he addressed the merchants, saying:
"My beloved son is just like your sons."
"If you should engage in unwholesome or unbeneficial matters, you must offer counsel and admonition so that you do not commit evil.
At that time, all the merchants respectfully agreed, and he further told his son:
"When you hear my words, you should carry them out; likewise, if the merchants give instruction, you should follow it as you would my own words."
Do not go at the front, nor do go at the rear. Why is this?
Because there may be violent bandits, or those who are weak in strength.
Those who are brave and strong came to the front of the merchants,
while those who were weak in strength followed from behind.
If the merchant leader were harmed, the entire caravan would be destroyed.
When the son had heard his father speak these words, the father further called the two slaves born in the household:
"Listen, you two! Neither of you shall ever leave my son on your own accord."
The two slaves replied,
“Truly as Your Majesty says!
Truly as Your Majesty says!”
The elder further reflected:
"What vehicle should my son ride? If I give him an elephant or a horse, it will consume a great deal of fodder."
"It would be more convenient for him to travel by donkey.
Having thought this, he immediately prepared a donkey carriage and sent him off, ensuring that all necessary provisions for the journey were fully provided.
The elder’s son went to his mother and said to her, "Mother!
I am now going to sea to gather treasures."
When his mother heard this, she became bewildered and fainted with grief, weeping as she urged him not to go,
asking, "When shall I see you again?
Because her son had become angry, he replied:
"We shall see one another in the woeful realms.
The mother replied to her son, "The words you have uttered are extremely coarse, foul, and unwholesome; you ought to repent so that your transgression may be diminished."
He immediately repented before his mother.
Having finished repenting, he mounted his vehicle and set out.
At that time, the various Brahmins, having performed auspicious prayers and blessings for him, took all the necessary goods and merchandise and departed with them.
Traveling gradually by stages, he passed through countless villages and cities before finally reaching the great ocean.
There, together with five hundred merchants, he took five hundred gold coins to hire a ship and five mariners:
one to hold the helm, one to know when to advance, one to know when to retreat, one to repair the vessel, and one to distinguish the waters.
Once they had finished their preparations, they offered prayers again and again.
At that time, the elder’s son, the caravan leader, beat the drum to proclaim his command and discourse upon the matters of good and ill fortune within the ocean.
Once the ship had departed, they reached the place of treasures and took a great quantity of precious goods; then, returning safely, they arrived back at the shore.
At that time, the merchant leader, the son of the elder, stayed apart in one location on the sandy beach, where he calculated with two household servants the expenditures for their coming and going.
The son of the householder said to his own servant:
"Dāsaka! Go and see what the merchants are doing now."
The slave went to look urgently and saw that the merchants were all sleeping; he then fell asleep as well.
Later, the elder’s son ordered Guhyaka to go and see what the merchants were doing now.
At that time, when Bhallika saw that all the merchants had completed their preparations and were about to set out with their pack animals,
Dāsaka said to him: "Bhallika, give the word."
Bālaka then said, "Dāsaka, report this to the caravan leader.
At that time, the two servants departed with the merchants.
When dawn had broken, the two servants, not seeing the elder’s son anywhere as they searched east and west,
asked the merchants, "Where is the elder’s son now?"
Some replied, "In front," while others said:
"He was behind. Though they all searched, they could not find him.
Each of the merchants said to one another:
"It is utterly improper for us to have abandoned the caravan leader; we must go and seek him immediately.
At that time, some of the merchants said, "This road is extremely perilous; if we go to search for the caravan leader, we shall all perish."
However, the merchant leader could not be found despite our search.
We devised a plan together: when we reached home and our father asked about the merchant leader, the one walking in front was to say, "The merchant leader is behind."
If asked about those who followed behind, one should say,
"The merchant leader was in front.
However, one must not say:
"The merchant leader has been lost!
Having said this, they gradually arrived at their home village.
When the elder Brahmadatta heard that the merchants had arrived, he went forward with joy and asked the people:
"Where is my son? The one walking ahead replied,
"He is behind."
The one who was behind said to him,
"Move forward.
Then the Brahmin Rishi thought to himself:
"These people have deceived me; has my son died, or has he been lost?
At that time, the elder, devoid of hope, was overcome with great anguish, and his kinsmen gathered together, weeping all at once.
The multitude all went to the house of the elder and wailed aloud.
Because they wept so profusely, both the elder and his wife became blind; furthermore, people from all directions came to know that the elder’s son had perished and was lost at sea.

The elder Brahmadatta had long worn the garments of mourning; during his son's lifetime, he gave away all the shoes, clothing, documents, and articles of personal use to the village shrines, and then made this vow:
"If my son’s life remains, may he reach wherever he is in safety and with speed."
"If my body has already died, may I be reborn in a superior realm.

While the elder’s son was asleep, he was awakened by the sun shining upon his body; having woken up, he found that the sand had been blown over by the wind so that he could no longer see the path, and he did not know where the merchants had gone.
He immediately mounted a donkey and set out.
The donkey, realizing it was not the old road, proceeded slowly.
Because the donkey walked so slowly, the elder’s son struck it with a staff; beaten and exhausted, the donkey could no longer go on.
The elder’s son further reflected:
"Who could bear to see such suffering and lack compassion by beating this donkey again?
He then proceeded on foot himself, driving the donkey away.
He saw an iron city; the city was vast, its walls exceedingly high, and its interior spacious.

Upon reaching the city gate, he saw a man whose body was tall and large, black in color with red eyes, his entire body covered in hair, and his belly coarse and massive; he was most terrifying and stood there grasping a staff.
Then the son of the householder asked the man, saying: "O man!
Is there water here?"
He remained silent and did not speak.
Having finished his questioning, the son of the householder entered the city.
Overcome by thirst, he wandered aimlessly from east to west in search of water; yet finding none at all, and his search proving fruitless, he finally cried out in a loud voice:
“Water! Water!

At that time, five hundred hungry ghosts arrived all at once; they resembled charred wooden pillars, with their own hair covering their bodies, throats like the eye of a needle, and bellies like great mountains, with flames erupting from every joint, blazing fiercely and glowing intensely. They addressed the caravan leader, saying:
"You possess great compassion; please give us water to drink, for we are tormented by thirst.
The son of the elder replied, "It was because I was tormented by thirst that I entered this city seeking water."
The hungry ghosts replied, "This is a city of hungry ghosts; where could one find water?
For twelve years, we have not even heard the name of water."
The son of the householder asked,
"What sinful karma did you commit to be born here?
The hungry ghost replied:
"The people of Jambudvīpa are generally prone to lack faith; if I were to speak now, you too would not believe me.
The son of the householder replied, "I have witnessed this with my own eyes right before me; how could I not believe it?"
At that time, the hungry ghost spoke in verse:
"I once reviled others and was constantly full of anger; I was stingy and grudged my wealth, refusing to give it to others.
I never practiced the act of giving; Due to the karma of these causes, I have been born as a hungry ghost."
At that time, the son of the elder gave rise to a mind of weary detachment from afflictions and immediately hurried out of the city, saying to that man:
"You must tell me: is this a city of hungry ghosts?"
"I shall not enter," the man replied.
"O caravan leader!"
"Can you see or hear of anyone else who has entered the city of hungry ghosts and emerged again?
It is because you possess great merit and majestic power that you have now been able to emerge once more.
Go in peace!"
"Go well! Then the son of the elder gradually proceeded forward, and when the sun was about to set, he beheld the site of a celestial palace.
There was a deva-son, accompanied by four celestial maidens, who were together enjoying themselves in pleasure and play within the palace.
Seeing the son of the householder from afar, that deity said to him:
"May you, O merchant leader, be free from illness.
Are you not hungry or thirsty?"
He replied, "I am indeed very hungry and thirsty! Thereupon,
the deva-son immediately had the merchant leader bathe, provided him with exquisite food and drink, and they stayed overnight.

When dawn had broken and the sun rose, that palace underwent a transformation: the four celestial maidens previously there changed into brindled dogs, seized this deva-son, and, covering his face, threw him onto a bed of glowing red-hot iron; as fierce flames streamed like falling stars, they devoured the flesh of his back.
Again, when evening arrived and the sun was about to set, it transformed back into a celestial palace, and the dog likewise transformed into a celestial maiden.
Having witnessed this with his own eyes, the elder’s son was deeply struck by its strangeness and immediately asked that deva-son:
"What karma did you perform to be born in this place?"
The devaputra replied,
“O caravan leader!
The people of Jambudvīpa are generally difficult to convince.”
The son of the householder said, "I have witnessed this with my own eyes now; why should I not believe it?
At that time, the devaputra recounted his past karmic conditions, answering in verse:
"In former times, by day I took the lives of others, But at night I maintained the precepts and practiced diligently;
By these causes and conditions, I was born here, And now I experience the fruits of such mixed good and evil karma."
When the son of the elder had heard this verse, he asked,
"What is the meaning of this verse?
The devaputra replied:
“O Caravan Leader!
In the past, when I was in the village of Vatsa, I was a butcher; I constantly sustained my body by killing sheep and selling their meat.”
At that time, there was a noble bhikṣu named Kātyāyana who exhorted me to repent and desist from such karma, saying that it would never come to an end.
When my exhortations were unsuccessful, the noble one further urged me to observe the precepts throughout the night.
I immediately followed these instructions.
Because of this karma, I suffer during the day;
yet because I observed the precepts at night, I now receive such a joyful retribution at night.
"O Merchant Leader!
If you reach that village and see my sons and daughters, speak on my behalf:
'I have seen your father undergoing extreme retribution for his suffering; you must now repent and desist from this karma.'"
Then the son of the elder said,
"You yourself have just stated that the people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to transform and difficult to inspire with faith.
The devaputra replied:
"Take this letter and convey my words to my son:
'Beneath the ground where the sheep were slaughtered, there is a jar of gold. You may dig it up and enjoy it as you please; thus you shall naturally find happiness.'"
Furthermore, you should from time to time make offerings to the noble Kātyāyana, who is a field of merit for gods and humans.
When making such offerings, at the time of giving, you should invoke my name and pray that your transgressions may be extinguished.
At that time, having heard these words, the merchant leader gradually proceeded forward and again saw a celestial palace.
There was a deva-son sporting joyfully with various heavenly maidens; seeing the son of the elder from afar, he addressed him, saying:
"Merchant leader!
"I hope you are free from illness; have you not suffered from hunger and thirst?
The son of the elder replied, "I am hungry and thirsty."
The deva-son immediately had him bathe, provided him with various foods and drinks, and settled him for restful sleep.
When evening arrived, the celestial palace transformed once more; the celestial maidens became great serpents that coiled around the deva-son’s body and devoured his brain from all sides.
When sunrise arrived, he returned to his celestial palace, assuming the form of a deva king and celestial maidens.
The merchant leader, struck by this marvel, asked that deva king:
"What karma did you previously create to be born here?"
The devaputra replied, "The people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to transform and difficult to inspire with faith; I cannot speak [to them].
Then the son of the householder answered:
"I have seen this with my own eyes; how could I lack faith?
At that time, the devaputra spoke these verses:
"Sleeping at night with another's wife, Yet guarding one's *śīla* by day; How can such a person, who acts thus, Not fall into the Avīci hell?"
"Due to the fruit of these karmic causes, one receives such retributions of good and evil.
At that time, the son of the elder asked:
"What is the meaning of this statement?"
The devaputra replied, “In the past,
while I was living in the village of Vatsa, I constantly engaged in sexual misconduct and violated the wives of others.
Later, I encountered the noble Kātyāyana, who exhorted me to repent for the unrighteous and evil karma I had committed.”
Because I did not cease this practice, the Noble One further said:
"Since you do not cease it permanently, you observe the precepts by day but commit non-virtuous acts at night.
Due to these circumstances, I experience celestial bliss by day and undergo the retribution of suffering by night.
"Excellent, son of a householder!
Go to that village and report this to my son on my behalf:
'I saw your father and spoke these words to him.'"
"I have committed this karma in a previous life by violating another's wife, and thus I am undergoing the sufferings of hell.
At that time, the son of the elder said, "The people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to transform and difficult to convince; how could they ever be willing to accept this?"
The devaputra replied: "If they do not believe you, tell them:
'During my lifetime, beneath the ground of the fire-pit, there are two jars of gold; you should dig them up and enjoy happiness for yourselves.'"

Furthermore, from time to time, they made offerings to Mahākātyāyana, who is honored by both humans and devas, and made a great vow, saying: "May my name be invoked so that my transgressions may be eliminated and I may be reborn in a favorable realm."
At that time, the son of the elder accepted these words and proceeded further. Not long after he had gone, he saw from afar yet another garden park.
Within it was a lion throne, upon which sat a woman whose countenance was exquisite and lovely, a sight pleasing to all who beheld her.
At each of the four legs of the seat sat a hungry ghost, bound to the leg and remaining there.
At that time, the woman saw the son of the elder approaching from afar and said to him:
"O Merchant Leader!
"Are you free from illness and have little affliction?
Do you suffer from hunger or thirst? He replied:
"I am very hungry and thirsty!
Then that woman said to the son of the elder,
"I shall give you some drinks."
"You should make a vow:
'The drink I am now giving must not be given to these four hungry ghosts.
The son of the householder replied:
"I respectfully accept what you have said.

Having been granted the provision of gruel and exquisite food and drink, the woman then entered a room and remained there, concealing her body, desiring to manifest the karmic retribution of a hungry ghost.
The hungry ghosts then said to the son of the elder,
"Out of your great compassion, we pray that you grant us a small amount of food and drink.
Moved by pity, the son of the elder immediately threw the food to them.
The food obtained by the first becomes a glowing mass of iron;
that obtained by the second becomes parched grain chaff;
and that obtained by the third becomes impure pus and blood.
Upon obtaining food for the fourth time, he instead returned to devouring his own flesh and blood.

At that moment, the hungry ghosts who had swallowed hot iron balls were burning with such foul stench that when the woman smelled the odor, she cried out in a loud voice and said to the son of the elder:
"What you have done is most unreasonable; you ought not to give him food and drink."
The elder’s son replied, “Sister!
Since he saw me and sought [my help], compassion arose in his heart; how could I not give it to him?”
Then the woman said:
"My heart of compassion is even greater than yours.
However, as for these hungry ghosts:"
"The first is my husband; the second is my son; the third is my daughter-in-law; and the fourth is my domestic slave.
At that time, the elder’s son asked:
"What sins did you commit to be born here?"
The woman said, "The people of Jambudvīpa are difficult to transform and difficult to inspire with faith; what benefit would there be in speaking?
The son of the elder replied:
"I see this clearly before my eyes; how could I not believe it? Then the woman said:

"In the past, in the village of Vatsapāla, I was once the daughter of a brahmin. On the occasion of the festival of Jupiter (Bṛhaspati), food was prepared at our home. At that time, the noble Kātyāyana, who is honored by both humans and devas, came to beg for alms."
I felt great joy and offered her a full alms-bowl of food.
I then thought to myself:
"I should now inform my husband, hoping that he might give rise to sympathetic joy regarding this cause for giving food."
Her husband, filled with anger toward his wife, said:
"We have not yet made offerings to the brahmins; for what reason do you first give alms to these shaven-headed men?
Why do you not give them glowing iron balls instead?"
Since his own wishes were not fulfilled, he next exhorted his son; the son replied in turn:
"Why do you not eat the chaff of that barley?"
"Later, I sent a servant to deliver food to my relatives. Having received the food, the servant ate the finest and most excellent portions for himself while on the road.
When he returned, I questioned him, and the servant then denied it, saying:
'If I have eaten it while on the road, may I eat the pus and blood from my own body!'"
Later, when her relatives again brought food, the daughter-in-law stole it.
When I questioned her about this, she replied,
"I did not eat!"
"If you eat, I vow to eat my own flesh. He said,
"O Merchant Leader!"
"Those who were his husband, son, wife, and servant are these very hungry ghosts; all because of their own actions, they now suffer as hungry ghosts."
"Because I gave a single meal to the noble Kātyāyana and spoke these words:
'If you receive the fruit of this merit, I shall see it with my own eyes.'"
"Previously, I practiced giving to Kātyāyana, who is honored by gods and humans, and I ought to have been reborn in the celestial palace of Śakra;
however, because I made an evil vow, I have now fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts."
"O Merchant Lord!
If you go to visit the village of Vatsapallī, I have a daughter who lives there as a courtesan. I pray that you will kindly inform her, saying:

'Your parents, elder brother, sister-in-law, and slave are all fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts, suffering there. Because they committed evil in the past, they now undergo this suffering. You should now repent; do not commit such evil, lest you too must suffer the retribution.'"
The son of the elder said:
"The people of Jambudvīpa are generally difficult to convince; they will not accept my words. He spoke thus.
"O Caravan Leader!
If he does not believe you, you should tell him:
'Previously, beneath my bed, there were four jars of gold along with a golden staff and a golden water-pitcher; you should go and take them out, and enjoy the golden jars as you please.'"

Furthermore, you must from time to time offer exquisite food and drink to Kātyāyana, who is renowned among gods and men, while reciting my name so that I may obtain merit and my transgressions may be lightened.
When the son of the householder had heard these words, he took his leave and entered his room to sleep.
At that time, the various spirits said to one another, "You should know:
while this son of the householder is fast asleep, you must carry him away and place him upon the spirit-couch in the village of Vasoṣa."
Then the various spirits, following his words, led him away.

At that time, when the dawn had broken and the sun was about to rise, the merchant leader woke up and saw that upon all the beds, small stools, shoes, and other articles of equipment, there were his names inscribed.
Reading it in sequence, he saw these words:
"Regarding this object I now bestow as a gift, I pray that my son may return soon.
Should he die, I pray that wherever he is reborn, all these objects shall follow him."
Having witnessed this event, he reflected:
"Since my parents already know that I am dead, what need is there for me to remain?
It would be fitting to go to the noble Kātyāyana and leave the household life to practice the holy life."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where Katyayana was.
At that time, the Venerable Katyayana saw the son of the householder coming from afar; having seen him, he addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, merchant leader!"
"Do you now perceive these faults and afflictions of birth and death?
He replied, "Noble One!"
"I have now seen it," he said.
He then further addressed him:
"I pray that you will allow me to go forth as a renunciant to serve the Noble One, severing lust, anger, and delusion, and practicing the holy life."
Then the Venerable Kātyāyana said:
"You should first deliver his message, and only after that may you come to receive ordination. He replied:
"So be it! Having heard the words of the Noble One, he immediately went to that village to the place where the sheep were being slaughtered; arriving at the man's location, he said to him:
"Do you know this now?"
"In the midst of the evil realms, I once beheld your father, who sent this message to you:
'You should turn back from this unrighteous act of killing sheep. He then replied:
"It has been twelve years since my father passed away; how could there be news transmitted from another realm? Did you hear this from someone else, or did you see it yourself?
He replied, "I have come here from the woeful realms."
If you do not believe this, your father said:

"Beneath the ground where you slaughter sheep, there is a golden jar. Dig it up and take that gold for your own use; furthermore, from time to time, provide food as an offering to the noble Kātyāyana, and while doing so, praise my name and pray that my karmic offenses may be extinguished."
"However, this butcher immediately dug beneath the ground and found a golden jar, thereby knowing it was a sign of verification.
At that time, the son of the elder went once more to visit the son of the profligate; having arrived, he said to him:
'I saw your father and was instructed by him to inform you of this matter:'"
"The karmic fruit of the deeds I have committed has ripened, and I am now experiencing manifold sufferings. The man replied,
"It has been twelve years since my father passed away."
Did you come here from another life?
Or did you hear it from someone else?
Or did you see it yourself?
The elder’s son said,
“I have come from among the hungry ghosts and have witnessed these events in their entirety.
If you do not believe me, your father will testify to it.”

"Under the fire-pit where you tend the flames, there are two golden jars; you should dig them up for your own use, and take one portion to offer as a single lump of food from time to time to the noble Kātyāyana, while praising my name and wishing that my karmic offenses may be extinguished."
The son immediately dug into the ground and found a golden jar; only then did he realize it was a manifest sign.
At that time, the elder’s son went again to the courtesan’s place and said to her:

“You should also know this: I have seen you, your parents, your brother, your sister-in-law, and your servant in the miserable realms. I have sent word to inform you so that you may urgently repent for your past evil deeds.”
He replied to the merchant leader, saying:
"It has been twelve years since they both died; who has seen or heard from them?
From where have you come?"
He replied: "I have come from hell.
If you do not believe me, ask your parents: [they will confirm it]."
"Under each of the four legs of the bed where I sleep lies a golden jar, and within each is a golden staff and a water-pitcher.

You may dig them up and enjoy them as you please; furthermore, from time to time, offer them to the noble Kātyāyana, who is honored by both gods and humans, and praise my name, vowing that my transgressions may be extinguished."
He immediately dug into the ground, and there was a letter from the Tathāgata exactly as described.
At that time, the son of the elder smiled and said,
"Everyone believes in gold, but they do not believe my words."
As he smiled, his teeth were revealed; when the woman saw his golden teeth, she realized that this man was the son of that elder, and she asked:
"Noble one! Are you not indeed the son of the Brahmin?"
He replied, "Everyone says it was me.
The girl immediately ran to her home and urgently informed her parents.
Upon hearing this, his parents were still unable to believe it.
The elder’s son went to their home himself and made a coughing sound.
His parents became suspicious and realized it was their son; they immediately took him by the head and wailed aloud with great lamentation.
The parents had been blind from birth, but through weeping, their cataracts were cleared away and they were able to see their son’s face.
At that time, the elder’s son said to his parents, "I wish to leave the home life; I pray you grant me permission."
His parents replied, "Because you have been blind in both eyes, we shall not allow you to leave the household life as long as we remain alive; once we have both passed away, you may do as you wish."
At that time, although the elder’s son remained at home, he constantly studied, recited, and chanted, until he eventually realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).

He then explained the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to his parents; having heard it, they used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty-fold mountain of the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Later, when both his parents had passed away, the elder’s son, out of grief, sorrow, and longing for his parents due to their separation, extensively practiced giving and cultivated various meritorious deeds. He then went to where the noble Kātyāyana was, prostrated with his head at the noble one's feet, and said:
"Noble One!..."
"I wish to go forth as a renunciant within this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, to practice the holy life, and to receive full ordination.
When the Noble One had thus observed him, he immediately granted Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa the going forth; while he was a śrāmaṇera, he realized the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
At that time, the place where he resided was a remote border region with few bhikṣus; it was difficult to receive full ordination, so he remained a śrāmaṇera.
He was instructed in all the practices of a śrāmaṇera and subsequently realized the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that there are two great assemblies each year, at which all bhikṣus gather together.
These two times are the end of spring and the end of summer.
All the assemblies of śrāvakas, both great and small, gathered like clouds from all directions.
The venerable and noble Kātyāyana’s disciples, along with various bhikṣus, had been observing the three-month rains retreat in other locations.

When the summer retreat had concluded and he had finished washing his robes, he put on his garments, took up his bowl, and traveled by stages until he reached the village of Vāsavagrāmaka, where the quorum of ten monks was finally completed.
At that time, the Venerable Kātyāyana immediately conferred full ordination upon Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.

Once he had received full ordination (*upasampadā*), all the rules of discipline (*vinaya*) were taught to him; he severed all afflictions (*kleśa*) and realized the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*).
Having attained this fruit, he became worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of gods and humans, as described at length above.
Then the bhikṣus went to the venerable Kātyāyana and said to him: "Venerable One!
Having resided here for some time and performed all the services and duties required to honor the Venerable One, we now wish to pay our respects to the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One."
The Noble One replied,
"Very well, follow me!
Having received this permission, he took up his robes and bowl and proceeded toward the city of Śrāvastī.
Then the venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed Kātyāyana, saying: "Upādhyāya!..."
I have a request to submit, and I pray that you will grant me your permission.
At present, I have seen only my upādhyāya, but I have not yet seen the Blessed One.
Although I have seen the Dharma-body, I have not yet seen the form-body.
"If my preceptor would permit me to see the physical marks and signs of the Tathāgata’s form-body, I too wish to go now.
At that time, the noble Kātyāyana said to Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are difficult to encounter."
"We have met after a long time, like the udumbara flower.
Now that you wish to depart, you should know the proper time. Kātyāyana replied:
"When you have reached the Blessed One's presence, prostrate yourself at his feet on my behalf and inquire after the Blessed One:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light in your movements and dwelling in comfort and ease?'"
Carrying these five matters with him, he went to inform the World-Honored One:
"The village of Vatsa is a remote region; it is difficult to find a quorum of ten for one who wishes to receive full ordination."
Furthermore, the people of that country always consider bathing with water to be purification.
The ground there is hard and firm; when oxen walk upon it, they leave footprints, unlike the soft soil found in other countries.
Furthermore, the people of the eastern countries use bedding such as the skins of rams, deer, and oxen.

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has sent a robe to another bhikṣu; having heard that the robe is on its way but it has not yet reached his hands, he fears he may incur the offense of "discarding after ten days have passed. Not knowing what to do, [he asks].
"I shall report this request in detail to the World-Honored One; having received the World-Honored One’s instruction, I shall reverently carry it out.

At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa focused his mind with single-minded devotion. Having taken leave of his teacher, he stayed overnight in that village. When the night had passed and morning dawned, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded by stages.
Having finished his almsround, after the meal, he took leave of his host; once he had returned his bedding and arranged his robes and bowl, he set out for Śrāvastī, traveling along the road.

Passing through various villages, he finally reached that city and arrived at the Jeta Grove; having set aside his robes and bowl and washed his hands and feet, he went immediately to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly, as well as for the devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others.
When the Buddha saw from afar that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was coming from a distant land, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You may prepare a bed, mattress, and bedding for Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa within the room."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately went to prepare the bed and bedding.
Once they were laid out, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"May the Noble One know that the time has come."

Having washed his feet, the Buddha entered his dwelling and lay down on his right side with one foot upon the other, assuming the lion’s posture of luminosity, maintaining right mindfulness and forming this mental resolve: "I shall rise at the proper time."

At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, having washed his feet outside the gate of the monastery, entered his cell and settled himself; as before, he lay down on his right side, maintaining the posture of light and reflecting that he would rise early.
Maintaining such mental attention, he remained silent throughout the night without uttering a single word.
When the night had passed, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa sat down cross-legged, straightened his body, concentrated his mind, and brought right mindfulness to the fore.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa:
“You may recite the sūtras and vinaya that I have spoken, just as they were spoken when I attained enlightenment.
He then instructed him to recite the sūtra; once Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had finished reciting it, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
The sūtra you recite is exceedingly pure and subtle.
At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa immediately had this thought:
“Upādhyāya! If you wish for me to make a request, now is precisely the right time.
Regarding the matter you have asked about, Upādhyāya, I shall now make that request.”
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“Venerable Sir!

In my residence, the village of Vatsapallī in the country of Aśmāparāntaka, which is a remote border region, there is the noble Kātyāyana, who is my preceptor. He bows his head in prostration at the Buddha’s feet and inquires after the World-Honored One’s health.”
"I hope you have little illness and little affliction, and that you dwell in lightness, ease, and comfort.
Furthermore, I ask the World-Honored One about five matters:
That country is a frontier region, and it is extremely difficult for a group of ten to perform the full ordination there."
Furthermore, the people of that country constantly practice bathing as their means of purification.
The soil of that land is extremely harsh and hard; once the hoofprints of oxen have been dried by the sun, people cannot walk upon them, which is unlike other countries.
In that country, they commonly use such bedding:
woolen mats, sheepskins, deer skins, ox hides, and the skins of wild goats, which serve as their bedding.

If a bhikṣu sends a robe to another bhikṣu, and hears that a robe is coming but it has not yet entered his hands, and ten days pass such that he fears he will incur an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), what should he do?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa:
"What you have asked is not the right time; I shall not speak of it now, so let this matter rest for a while."
"You should ask your questions among the assembly; I shall resolve your doubts for you within this great multitude.
When dawn arrived, the Buddha rose and took his seat among the assembly.
Once the Buddha had sat down, the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and said:
"In the border country to the east, in the village of Vāsavagrāma, dwells the noble Kātyāyana; he is my upādhyāya. He bows his head to the Buddha’s feet and inquires after the World-Honored One:
‘Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your daily activities? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?’"
In the border regions of that country, it is difficult to find a quorum of ten monks for those wishing to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The people of that country habitually consider bathing with water alone to be purification.
The soil within this country is extremely hard; when oxen walk upon it, their footprints dry up under the sun's heat so that people cannot pass over them, which is unlike other countries.
Furthermore, according to the laws of the country, such bedding materials are used—namely, the skins of sheep, goats, deer, oxen, and rams—as bedding.

A bhikṣu sent a messenger to give robes to another bhikṣu. Upon hearing that the robes were coming, but before they had arrived, ten days passed; fearing he might commit an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika), he did not know what to do.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"From now on, it is permitted for bhikṣus in frontier regions to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) with a quorum of five bhikṣus who are experts in the Vinaya."

In frontier regions where the terrain is harsh, it is permitted to wear single-layered leather sandals; double or triple layers are not allowed. If the soles become worn through, they should be repaired.
If a bhikṣu sends a messenger to deliver robes to another bhikṣu, and that recipient has not yet received the robes, there is no offense regarding the forfeiture of the transgression.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli was present in the assembly; he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One!"

When [the Buddha] was about to permit the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*) by a group of five who uphold the Vinaya in the border regions, [the monks] did not know from where those border regions began.
The Buddha said:
"To the east of here lies the Bhaṇḍa Forest; there is a body of water called Bhaṇḍa. From this point onward, it is known as the border countries."
In the south there is a country named Śrāvastī, and there is also a river named Śrāvastī; beyond this area, it is likewise called a border region.
To the west there is a country named Sūttanu; the Brahmin village of Upasūttanu is called a border region beyond this.
To the north there is a mountain named Uśīra; the area beyond this mountain is called a border region.
The bhikṣus, having conceived a doubt, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What karma did this bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa previously create?"

Born into a family of great wealth and nobility with immeasurable riches and treasures, while still in the mother’s womb, there naturally appeared upon his ears these wondrous jeweled earrings, worth an incalculable sum.
Furthermore, he attained the full ordination of a bhikṣu; yet, without seeing the World-Honored One, he attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) and severed all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa has experienced the results of his own past karma; what he did himself, he must receive himself."
When causes and conditions converge, they are like a torrential flood that must inevitably be endured.

Now that these conditions have finally met, one must receive this retribution; furthermore, neither earth, water, fire, nor wind can destroy the fruit of karmic retribution, for the body must experience it itself.
As it is said in a verse:
"Even if a hundred eons were to pass, The karma one has created does not perish.
When causes and conditions meet, One must experience the retribution oneself."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles, who resided at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near Vārāṇasī."

In that country there was a king named Kṛki who ruled through righteous transformation; the population was flourishing, food and drink were abundant, and free from all decline and affliction, everyone was entirely at peace and happy.
Free from thieves and fear, he was fully endowed with all things and lacked for nothing; he ruled the world according to the Dharma.
That king had a son named Sujāta, whom he established as the crown prince.
When the Tathāgata Kāśyapa had completed his work of conversion, he entered parinirvāṇa like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted.

King Kṛkin then took fragrant wood to cremate him and used cow’s milk to extinguish the flames. He collected the śarīras and fashioned a casket from four kinds of precious gems. At a crossroads, he erected a stūpa made of the seven treasures, one krośa in height, wherein he enshrined the śarīras.
All the tribute goods from the eastern borders of that kingdom were entirely offered to the stūpa.
Later, when the king passed away, the crown prince was established as king; he then, together with his various ministers, inspected the storehouses to determine the quantity of the items remaining.
He also saw that all the tribute goods produced from the eastern borders of the kingdom were being bestowed upon the stupa.
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"There are previously existing items belonging to the stupa that were bestowed by former kings; should these not be reclaimed?"
The new king replied:
"The deeds performed by my late father, the former king, were like those of Śakra or Brahmā, the King of Devas; how could I now dare to take back these objects?"
However, none of the ministers believed in or delighted in the Buddha-dharma; they collectively thought to themselves:
"We must now devise a skillful means to reclaim all the goods intended for the stupa."
He immediately closed the eastern gate of the city so that no goods whatsoever could enter; consequently, the colors of the stupa flaked off and it fell entirely into ruin.
At that time, a merchant leader from the north arrived in this country with his caravan and stayed beside the stupa.

At that time, while the merchant leader was paying homage at the stūpa, he saw that the stūpa was in a state of ruin. He also saw a woman there who, having no sons or daughters, was sweeping and making offerings.
That woman, upon seeing the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, gave rise to the resolve for awakening and received instruction from that Buddha.
The merchant leader asked the girl,
"Whose stūpa is this?
The girl then related the causal circumstances in detail:
"This is the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha.

Upon hearing this, the merchant leader felt great joy; he immediately removed his earrings and offered them to the woman, instructing her to sell them and use the proceeds for the restoration of the stūpa, saying:
"When I return, I shall make further offerings."
Having received them, the woman immediately adorned herself.

When the merchant leader returned, he gazed upon that stūpa with inexhaustible devotion; thereupon, he conceived a resolute mind and further constructed jeweled parasols, banners, and streamers as offerings. He made this vow:
"By all the roots of goodness from my present offering to this stūpa of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, may I always attain wealth, nobility, and high status in whatever place I am born in the future."
"In the presence of the future Buddha, I vow to leave the household life, sever all afflictions, and realize the fruit of no-more-learning.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Who else could that merchant leader have been?"
This was none other than the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.

Because he made offerings to the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha, in every successive birth he was always born into a wealthy and noble family; even while in the womb, precious jeweled earrings would naturally appear upon his ears.
Furthermore, he vowed that in the future he would leave the household life, sever all afflictions, and attain the fruit of Arhatship.
Because he had uttered harsh words toward his mother, by the power of this karma, he beheld the various hells.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one performs white karma, one obtains a white retribution; if one performs black karma, one obtains a black retribution; and for mixed karma, there is a mixed retribution."
"O bhikṣus! You should abandon mixed and black karma, and you should cultivate white karma.
Thus he addressed the bhikṣus.
"This is my instruction.
When the bhikṣus had heard what the Buddha spoke, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
