At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Upānanda had recently gone forth into homelessness and was assigned a single bed, which was in a state of extreme decay.
Whenever he moved his body, the bed would creak; lying upon it, he did not dare to turn over for fear of making a noise.
Upānanda then thought to himself:
"If I do not beg for and have a better bed made, I shall no longer be worthy of the name Upānanda."
When morning dawned on the following day, he went to King Prasenajit.
The king said, "Welcome, Venerable Upānanda!"
"Are you able to sleep in peace?
He then replied to the king,
"Though I lie down to sleep, my mind is constantly filled with terror."
"Your Majesty knows for yourself that before I went forth into homelessness, I slept upon bedding of eight layers.

Now, although I have gone forth, being but a junior monk of few years' standing, I have been allotted a single broken bed; it makes a sound whenever touched, and I dare not turn over in sleep for fear of breaking it—this is truly a great hardship."
"How can one sleep in peace? The King said to Upānanda,
"Is it appropriate for you to lie upon such an eight-layered bedding?"
He then replied to the king: "I have.
This is entirely consistent with reason; where in the Buddha’s regulations is it forbidden to lie upon a bedding arrangement of eight layers?"
The king said, "If it is according to the Dharma, I now bestow it upon you; take it as you please.
He then spoke again to the king:
"I am not the king; how could I take the property of the royal household?
The King should send someone to deliver it to the monastery, and I shall accept it."
The king gave it to eight men; four carried the bedding and four carried the bed.
Having received it, Upānanda laughed joyfully and followed along.
On the road, there were various laypeople, Brahmins, and others who, seeing these beds and bedding, asked:
"Whose property is this? They replied:
"The King gave it.
He asked again,
"If you take this bed away, where will the King sleep?"
Upānanda replied, "I am permitted to sleep upon these beds and bedding in my own home.
When the laypeople heard this, they immediately began to mock and reproach him.
"This shaven-headed śramaṇa keeps such bedding and requisites for sensual pleasure!
Upānanda then went to the monastery, swept and sprinkled the courtyard, smeared it with cow dung, and spread out his beds and mats by the doorway.
When the Buddha arrived at the gate, Upānanda saw him approaching and joyfully said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Look at my bed!"
"Look at me lying on my bed!
Having seen this, the Buddha remained silent for a moment, then gathered the community of bhikṣus, took his seat, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one sits or lies upon a large bed, all manner of faults arise because of it."
"From this day forward, if a bhikṣu sits or lies upon a high or large bed, he shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
There was a householder who invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to a meal at his home and prepared a high seat for them.
At that time, Ānanda arrived at the house first and, seeing the high seat, said to the elder:
"This high seat is not in accordance with the Dharma; it should be removed immediately."
Just as he was about to remove it, the Buddha arrived at his house;
knowing [the situation], he asked intentionally, "What do you intend to do? Ānanda replied:
"Remove the improper seats.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "I have not prohibited the use of high beds in all places; rather, their use is permitted in the homes of laypeople."
"If one sits or lies down within the vihāra, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu from the south who, possessing only his three robes, came to the city of Śrāvastī to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
There was a leather mat used as a cushion for the body.
When Upānanda saw it, he immediately followed after him, offering greetings and praise; once the bhikṣu had rested for a moment, he then requested it from him, saying:
"O bhikṣu who lives on alms, would you be able to bestow this leather upon me?"
"I wish to travel among the various monasteries, and I always take him with me whenever I pass by a stūpa to circumambulate and pay homage to the holy sites.
He then replied, "Upānanda!"
"I am now offering this to you; are you able to go?
Upānanda replied, "Indeed, I have the strength to procure this hide; it shall not be difficult for me."
He said to Upānanda, "If that is the case, I will not give you the hide.
Upon hearing these words, he became angry and remained silent, thinking to himself:
“The Great King Pasenadi of Kosala has a cowherd named Bhaṇḍa; he was formerly an acquaintance of mine. He possesses a hide, and if I beg it from him, I shall certainly obtain it without doubt.”
Having formed this thought, he went to that place.

It happened to be the beginning of spring; a cow had given birth to a spotted calf that was exceedingly lovely, and as soon as Upānanda stroked the calf’s body with his hand, a feeling of affection arose within him.
Having seen this, Paṭṭa said to Upānanda, "Venerable One!
Do you require cow's milk?"
He replied, "There is no need; seeing this calf-skin, I find it very pleasing.
If I obtain this skin as a mat, it will suffice to support my body so that I may practice the Path in peace and security."
Bhaṭṭa replied: "Noble One, please return for now."
"I already know your intention.
Not long after he had departed, Pāṭaliputra immediately ordered someone to kill the calf and flay its skin, sending it to Upānanda.
Following these instructions, the man killed the calf and flayed its skin in the presence of the mother cow, then took the hide and delivered it to Upānanda.
However, when the mother cow saw her calf being led away with its hide, she cried out loudly and followed after it out of love for her child.
The man carrying the hide took it toward the Jetavana Monastery; having arrived and entered the monastery, the mother cow remained outside the gate.
When the Blessed One saw this cow, he knew the reason but asked Ānanda intentionally:
"For what reason has this cow been standing outside the gate for so long, making such a sound? Then Ānanda replied:
"Venerable Sir!
Because Upānanda killed a calf and took its hide to use as a bedding,
and because that calf was born of this very cow, the mother, out of her affection for her child, follows after her calf’s hide outside the gate."
At that time, the Blessed One thought to himself:
"A fault has arisen because of those hides.
He then went into the midst of the community of bhikṣus, took his seat, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Upānanda is foolish and lacks wisdom; for the sake of using leather, he has performed what is not the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Therefore, monks, from this day forward, you must no longer use leather.”
"If one uses leather, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
As the Blessed One said:
"A bhikṣu should not use leather."
There was a certain householder who invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to his home to provide offerings, yet he again used leather for his seats.
When this came to the Buddha’s attention, he said to Ānanda:
“One should not prohibit the use of leather in all circumstances; therefore, I permit its use when sitting in a layperson’s home, but it must not be used for lying down.”
"If one sits or lies down in a vihāra, it is not permitted;
if one makes such use of it, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
This occurred in Rājagṛha. At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa had been afflicted by constant illness ever since his ordination.
To all his kinsmen who came to him, he preached the Dharma before departing.
Once he had returned home, he spoke again to his wife:
"Today the noble Pilindavatsa preached the Dharma for me; it was as sweet as pure honey, with nothing to be discarded."
His wife replied, "The fruition of your past karma has ripened;
you have encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world and are able to hear the sublime Dharma.
The husband said:
"Why do you not listen? He replied,
"Because of my sense of shame, I am unable to go there to hear the Dharma."
"It would be most excellent if a noble one were to come here and preach for us.
Thereupon, the husband went to the place of Pilindavatsa and said to him, "Noble One!"
I have received the teaching of the Dharma, which has brought immeasurable benefit.
My wife is a woman; because she possesses a sense of modesty, she is unable to come here to hear the Dharma, yet she deeply longs to hear it.
"If the Noble One deigns to show his virtue and preach out of compassion, only then will this woman be able to hear the Dharma.
Then the Venerable Pilindavatsa said, "Since I went forth into homelessness, my body has been constantly ill; I am unable to go there."
That person replied, "Noble One!
We shall serve as attendants and carry him away."
He replied, "The World-Honored One has not yet permitted it.
He reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"For the sake of the bhikṣus who are aged or infirm, I shall permit them to ride in a carriage.
He then assembled the saṃgha of bhikṣus, took his seat in their midst, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"From this day forward, you shall ride in a carriage for the sake of what is beneficial.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus was also present in the assembly, and as the Blessed One had said:
"I permit the Venerable Pilindavatsa to ride in a carriage."
Surrounded by their attendants, they went to the house of the brahmin householder.

Upon hearing this, the group of six monks immediately fashioned various exquisite, painted jeweled carriages and rode upon them through the streets. They frequented the homes of laypeople and moved about with such arrogance that they treated others like blades of grass, paying no heed to those before or behind them.
A brahmin householder asked him: "Noble one!
For what reason are you riding?"
He replied, "The World-Honored One has permitted riding.
At that time, all the people spoke with universal derision, saying:
“You śramaṇas, you are driven by desire.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the World-Honored One said:
“Bhikṣus, since this fault has already occurred, you should not ride on horseback.”
There are two conditions under which it is permitted. What are these two?
First, being emaciated and weak; second, being old and sick.
"If there is a valid reason for this, I shall grant permission;
if one rides [a vehicle] without such a reason, they shall incur an offense against the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the countryside who encountered water on the road and was unable to carry his robes and bowl while swimming across.
Then the bhikṣus reported the circumstances to the Buddha in full. The World-Honored One told them:
"You bhikṣus, you should practice learning how to swim.
When the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had permitted them to learn swimming for the purpose of crossing water, they did so.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were crossing back and forth by swimming in the Śītā River.
Later, a householder’s daughter arrived at the riverbank; finding no boat to cross, she stood there for a long time in distress.
At that time, the six bhikṣus said to the women, "We shall ferry you across.

When the women saw that they were renunciants, they immediately placed their trust in them and crossed the river together. Once they reached the other shore, the monks then touched every limb and joint of the women's bodies while they were in the water, and having arrived at the far bank, they spoke to the women again.
"Come back; I shall ferry you across as well.
Then that woman said, "You shaven-headed man, you harbor a most wicked and malicious nature!"
"My husband does not even touch my limbs, let alone you," she said,
and immediately reviled and insulted him.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Whatever afflictions arise, they all stem from touching the bodies of women.
I shall now prohibit the bhikṣus from touching the bodies of women.
Having formed this thought, he assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them:
“O foolish group of six bhikṣus!

In many ways you have created sources of outflows, performing what is not the dharma of a śramaṇa, acting contrary to proper conduct, and unreasonably engaging in impure contact with the bodies of women.”
"From this day forward, none of you shall touch the body of a woman.
Should any do so, he shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

After the Blessed One had thus prohibited the bhikṣus from touching women, there was a lord of a city who, always fond of excellent gardens, groves, and ponds, went to a garden with his wife, children, and retinue, all elegantly adorned in their garments.
Among the crowd was a woman who, carrying a jar, went to the river to fetch water.
There was also a bhikṣu on the riverbank straining water to observe for insects.
The woman felt ashamed; seeing the bhikṣu at the edge of the path where she was taking water, she immediately moved far away and drew her water from a narrow, precipitous spot.
Once the water jar was full and he was about to lift it, the girl tripped and fell into the water, being carried away by the current.
At that moment, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a training rule that one must not touch the body of a woman."
"If anyone touches it, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣu abandoned her and did not rescue her. Her family, wondering why she was so late, searched for her and asked the bhikṣu:
"Did you see a woman carrying a jar to fetch water?"
He replied, “I saw him fall into the river and being carried away by the current. He said:

“Noble One! Out of compassion for sentient beings, you constantly observe even tiny insects within the water; how could it be right for you now to abandon and fail to rescue this woman who is drowning?”
The bhikṣu replied,
"The World-Honored One does not permit touching the body of a woman.
Having heard these words, she immediately began to revile and disparage him.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the World-Honored One declared:
"If there is a life-threatening danger, one must rescue them.
If they can save themselves, then release them as soon as you say 'release'."
At that time, when the bhikṣus took hold of her, they gave rise to defiled thoughts. The Buddha said:
"When you take hold of a woman, you should regard her with the perception of her as a mother, a daughter, or a sister, and rescue her so that she may emerge [from suffering]."
There were those who attempted to rescue him, but once he was submerged and exhausted, he was unable to regain consciousness. The Buddha said:
"He lay upon a mound of sand with his face turned downward."
At that time, the bhikṣus merely covered his face and lay him down before departing; consequently, he was devoured by crows, vultures, and jackals. The Buddha said:
"One must not depart after leaving [the body] unattended; one must certainly provide protection."
The bhikṣu guarded it, keeping it close to his side, whereupon a defiled thought arose. The Buddha said: "It should not be kept close;
you must guard it with mindfulness according to the occasion.
Because the bhikṣu was guarding it, he failed to eat at the proper time. The Buddha said:
"When the time for the bhikṣus' meal approaches, they should see the cowherds and shepherds and instruct them to guard the animals.
After eating, they must repeatedly check upon them to ascertain whether they are alive or dead."
At that time, the six bhikṣus were bathing at the banks of the Aciravatī River. There was a cow belonging to a certain householder’s family that habitually crossed the river.
On this occasion, the six bhikṣus each seized the tail of the milch cow and went back and forth across the river; as a result, the cow’s milk subsequently ceased to flow.
The elder rebuked the cowherd, who recounted the matter in detail; the elder then censured him.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this incident to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them:
"You should not grasp the tail of an ox while crossing a river."
"If anyone violates this, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
After the World-Honored One had thus prohibited it, [he declared]:
"One should not cross water by grasping the tail of an ox."
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who wished to cross a river, but as there was no boat or raft, they were unable to do so.
For this reason, they went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know that there are five things one may grasp to cross [a river]: namely, an elephant, a horse, a calf-ox, a cat-ox, and an air-bladder."
At that time, the six bhikṣus fashioned various kinds of elaborate decorations, painting the figures of men and women upon their leather air-cells as they crossed over.
The brahmins and householders all said to one another,
"What kind of principle is this?"
He replied, "The World-Honored One has granted me permission.
At that time, the brahmins, householders, and others all voiced their derision and reproach:
"This bald śramaṇa is oppressed by lustful desire.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!..."
One should not cross a river using various painted figures of men or women;
rather, one should place two kinds of flotation bags:
one of brownish color and one that is small.
While the Blessed One was preaching the Dharma, a bhikṣu came along the road and, seeing a black snake,
said, "I see a long one. The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus should wear wooden sandals. This occurred in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had constructed a magnificent new hall, adorned with various colorful paintings. He invited the bhikṣus to preach the Dharma and recite the sūtras therein, to rest after their meals, and to repair their robes; he also provided various lion thrones for them to sit upon.
At the place where the Dharma was being taught, there was at that time a bhikṣu who came wearing wooden sandals; he stepped upon the ground, causing it to be damaged.
Early one morning, when Anāthapiṇḍada went to pay homage to the World-Honored One, he saw that the ground had been trampled into pits and hollows by the wooden sandals.
He asked, "Noble One!"
"Has the King, along with his fourfold army, come here to stay the night? He replied, "No."
However, because the bhikṣus wore wooden sandals, they subsequently stepped on the ground and damaged it.
The householder criticized and disparaged this, and the Buddha said:
"You all have damaged the temple grounds by wearing wooden sandals."
"From this day forward, you must not possess wooden sandals.
Should you possess them, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
A bhikṣu who had been observing the rains retreat at home for three months found his leather sandals worn out and ruined.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If one is in a layperson's home, there is no offense in wearing wooden sandals.
At that time, faithful householders and brahmins offered wooden sandals to the bhikṣus, but none were willing to accept them, all saying:
"When the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, the non-Buddhist practitioners were the field of merit.
Now that the Buddha has appeared, you, O virtuous ones, are the field of merit; please accept this out of compassion for me."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"You should accept it; having accepted it, place it by the latrine for use.
A summary verse says:
Sandals made of bamboo leaves and reed ropes were permitted for protection;
formerly, one wore sandals adorned with leather, fastened with heavy straps and linings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"One must not use wooden sandals; one should instead take bamboo leaves to make sandals.
When the bhikṣus wore sandals made of bamboo leaves, various faults and afflictions arose. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not keep bamboo-leaf sandals; you should wear sandals made of *po* grass."
As these faults and afflictions arose once more, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You must not possess mats made of *tūla* grass.
You, bhikṣus, should wear sandals made of cord."
This again gave rise to further faults. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You must not keep rope sandals.

At that time, some bhikṣus suffered from wind-swelling (vāta-śotha) and ailments in their thighs; being tormented by the pain, they had to douse them with water, which caused their leather sandals to rot completely.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the World-Honored One told them: "O bhikṣus!
If you suffer from wind-induced swelling of both legs, you should wear corded sandals; do not harbor any doubt regarding this."

At that time, the youth Koṭikarṇa’s body was soft and supple; because the karmic retribution of his past deeds had matured, there were golden hairs on the soles of his feet, four finger-widths in length.
At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group saw him and said to one another:
"This boy is like a jar filled with fresh butter; now that he has gone forth in the Buddha's teaching, what can he possibly accomplish?"
Having heard this, the youth felt displeasure in his heart; he immediately went to where Ānanda was, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Venerable One!
Why do you single-mindedly and diligently seek to practice samādhi?"
He replied: "Venerable sir! As the Buddha has said:"
"Walking meditation is supreme.
He then went to a *śmaśāna* (cemetery) and prepared a place for walking meditation, where he practiced it.

Because he walked so much, the four-finger-width golden hairs on the soles of his feet all fell out, and both feet were chafed and broken, with blood flowing onto the ground. It was as if a butcher of sheep were moving from here to there, while crows followed behind to feed upon him.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that, before entering parinirvāṇa, they go from time to time to the riverbank for a stroll, as has been described.
Therefore, the World-Honored One traveled to this place, even unto the dwelling of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
The World-Honored One saw that blood was flowing from wherever Koṭīviṃśa had walked for meditation; knowing the cause, he intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Which bhikṣu is this who has been single-mindedly and diligently seeking supreme samādhi?"
Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“This is where Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa used to practice walking meditation.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! I now permit Koṭikarṇa to wear leather sandals with a single layer of sole; he must not wear those with two or three layers. If the sole should break, it shall be mended.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was and said to him:

“Venerable, the Buddha has permitted the wearing of single-layered leather sandals; one must not wear those of two or three layers. If the soles become worn through, they should be repaired. This is for the sake of wearing them with stability and for the cultivation of merit.”
He said, "Venerable One!
Did the Blessed One grant permission for all bhikṣus to wear it, or did he intend for me alone to wear it?"
Then Ānanda said: "World-Honored One!
When I saw you walking back and forth, blood was flowing from beneath your feet; therefore, I have directed that you wear it alone."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"Venerable sir!
Who would dare to disobey the Buddha's instruction?"
Nevertheless, you alone have been permitted to wear them, while other practitioners of the holy life who see this say:

"I have renounced my master and all my kinsmen, as well as abundant wealth, treasures, and palaces; having relinquished everything, I have gone forth into homelessness, yet you alone are permitted to wear leather sandals."
"If the Blessed One permits the entire community of bhikṣus to wear them collectively, I too shall wear them in accordance with the instruction;
if it is otherwise, I do not dare to wear them alone."
Ānanda went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter in detail. The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"From this day forward, I permit the community of bhikṣus to wear single-layered leather sandals; they must not wear those of two or three layers. If they become worn, they should be mended and worn."
Then the Venerable Ānanda assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"The Buddha has permitted the bhikṣus to wear single-layered leather sandals; they must not wear those of two or three layers. If they become worn, they should be mended and worn."
Among them was a certain mahallaka renunciant who, wearing sandals, headed toward the place for walking meditation. The World-Honored One said to him, "Stay away from my presence."
Having spoken these words, he immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"If I were still in the midst of lay life, you would have been permitted to wear leather sandals when seeing me."
"If you are alone in another place, you must not come to see me wearing leather sandals while among the community of bhikṣu śrāvakas.

As the Buddha had spoken, there was a certain bhikṣu who wished to wash his feet; however, the water jar was broken. He then washed his feet in a clean basin, filled his mouth with water, and moved about like a scorpion.
When the six bhikṣus saw this, they said,
"Are you dancing without hearing any sound? Thereupon,
the six bhikṣus immediately began to harmonize their voices with the music.
Another bhikṣu said, "Why are you acting so frivolously?
The group of six replied:
“Do you not see that this bhikṣu performs a dance without making any sound?
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One, knowing the reason, asked them anyway, and finally addressed the mahallaka bhikṣu:
“What were you thinking when you did this? The bhikṣu replied,
“I did it because I wished to avoid soiling my bedding.”
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If one acts in this manner for the sake of protecting bedding and seats, there is no fault.

I now permit the bhikṣus, for the sake of protecting bedding and seats, to wear single-layered leather sandals; they shall not wear double or triple layers. If they become worn or torn, they should be repaired."
The setting was the city of Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a certain mendicant bhikṣu.
A certain householder, moreover, had conceived deep faith and reverence for this bhikṣu.
At that time, a bhikṣu went barefoot; at the hour of dawn, he put on his robes and took up his bowl to enter the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
Since he was not wearing leather sandals, the elder saw that his feet were cracked and split, and said:
"Noble One!..."
"May you not wear leather sandals? He replied, "Worthy one!"
"I have no leather sandals.
He spoke again, saying, "Noble One!"
"Let us go together to the tanner's workshop; measure the size of your feet so that he may fashion you a leather sandal.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu went with him to the tanner's house and said, "O worthy one!"
"You may measure the feet of this renunciant and fashion a pair of leather sandals of that size to offer him.
The shoemaker, having measured his feet, then thought:
"This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas collects taxes by mere word."
"If I am to make it for you, we must set a distant date; you may not demand the payment immediately.
At that time, all the bhikṣus wore single-layered leather sandals.
That bhikṣu who went for alms went repeatedly to the tanner’s workshop, but as he could not obtain any,
he could no longer go there. Later, when that faithful householder saw that the bhikṣu still did not wear leather sandals, he asked him,
"For what reason do you not wear leather sandals?"
He replied, "I have not yet obtained them.
At that time, the elder went with the bhikṣu to a tanner's workshop and requested leather sandals.
The man replied, "I have no single-layered leather sandals, but many multi-layered ones;
take whichever you please. The mendicant bhikṣu responded:
"The Buddha does not permit the wearing of multi-layered leather sandals.
The householder said,
"I shall simply take them to my residence and remove all but one layer."

He accepted it immediately and took it to his dwelling; as soon as he sat down, intending to tear it open, the World-Honored One arrived and saw him. It is the constant law of all Buddhas to inquire knowingly about matters even though they are already understood, and so the Buddha asked: "What are you doing?"
He then answered in full detail, and the Buddha said:
"Do not do such a thing.
The World-Honored One further thought to himself:
"These faithful Brahmins, householders, and lay devotees offer many heavy leather sandals to my śrāvaka disciples; I should permit their wearing."
Having formed this thought, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"Now there is a householder who has offered a bhikṣu multi-layered leather sandals, yet that bhikṣu wishes to tear them apart to make them single-layered."
For this reason, I now permit the bhikṣus: if there is a householder who has previously worn leather sandals many times and offers them to a bhikṣu, he may accept and wear them.
Then the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bhadanta,
as the Buddha has said:..."
"I have heard that a householder once wore many layers of leather sandals.
I do not know what is meant by 'formerly used by a householder'.
The Buddha said:
"If a householder has previously worn [them] while walking seven or eight paces, these are called 'leather sandals that have been used.
The occasion was at Vaiśālī.
At that time, in this city, various kinds of leather sandals were being made; when they were worn, they sometimes produced the sound "kiki-nini" or the sound "isi-yisi-yisi."
As for the style of these leather sandals, some were made in the shape of ram's horns and others in the shape of bodhi trees; they were adorned with various colors and were worth five gold coins.

At that time, when the six bhikṣus saw someone wearing leather sandals, they would cast aside their own sandals, immediately trample upon the other person's sandals with their feet, push them over, and forcibly seize them, saying:
"May you, who have bestowed these leather sandals, always wear precious sandals in the future and enjoy the happiness of the heavenly realms."
At that time, the brahmins, householders, and others all felt resentment and shame, and they all mocked him together, so that the news spread far and wide:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have forcibly seized a man's sandals."
At that time, there was a brahmin who purchased a pair of leather sandals for a high price and thought to himself:
"When my daughter's son-in-law arrives, I shall give these to him to wear."

Before long, the husband arrived; once he had rested from his journey, she first provided him with a bath and anointed him with fragrant unguents, then adorned him with various necklaces and ornaments.
After he had eaten, she gave him these leather sandals and said:
"My son!..."
"I have used great effort to craft these sandals; you must guard them well so that they are not taken away by the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.

On the following day, the son-in-law put on these leather sandals and went out into the streets, where he saw a mendicant bhikṣu who, in the morning, had dressed and taken up his bowl to go on his alms-round in due order.
Seeing the bhikṣu, he became suspicious; having entered another house, the bhikṣu went there for alms.
As the man was leaving that place and heading toward another house, he said: "Noble one!"
"For what reason have you followed me hereafter?
I will certainly not give you my leather sandals. The bhikṣu replied:
“O noble one! I was begging for alms myself; I did not seek your leather sandals.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the World-Honored One then had this thought:
"Now this fault has arisen because of the adornment of leather sandals.
The World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and said:
"The group of six bhikṣus, seeing others wearing fine leather sandals, forcibly snatched them away from them; all the brahmins and householders have consequently censured and disparaged them."
"Therefore, monks, you should not wear leather sandals decorated with such colorful ornaments.
If you do so, you shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
This was the occasion at Śrāvastī, when [the Buddha] permitted the wearing of leather shoes.
At that time, as the bhikṣus were walking on leather sandals that had chafed their feet and caused sores,
some brāhmaṇas and householders saw them and spoke thus:
"Noble ones!..."
"Was your foot injured by an old crow?
He replied, "No,
it is merely that my leather shoes have worn out."
"Why do you not fasten your long sash?
He replied, "The World-Honored One has not yet permitted it."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I allow you to wear leather-strapped shoes.
This occurred while the Blessed One was at Rājagṛha; at that time, the bhikṣus were ascending Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had developed a sore on his big toe; he entered the city to beg for alms.
The Brahmins, householders, and others questioned him as they had done previously.
The Buddha permitted the wearing of heavy shoes.
However, when descending the mountain, they still damaged their heels; consequently, the Buddha permitted the wearing of linings on both sides.
A summary verse says:
Regarding straw sandals, leather shoes, and boots: fur-lined boots are permitted in cold snow;
if a hunter offers bear skin, one may accept it; and one should keep awls and knives for mending sandals.
The setting was the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, it was during a period of persistent rain; the bhikṣus, wearing green grass sandals, went out to beg for alms, and pustules as large as mustard seeds broke out all over their feet.
At that time, the brahmins and householders all asked:
"Venerable One!
For what reason do you have such sores upon your feet?"
He replied, "It was because of those straw sandals that this has come to pass.
Then the Brahmins and others said:
“Venerable One! Why do you not wear sandals? He replied:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted its use.
The World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to wear sandals with thick soles."
At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, long grass grew profusely along the streets and thoroughfares; when the bhikṣus walked upon it, their ankles were wounded.
The brahmins, householders, and others [complained], leading up to the Buddha’s words:
“I allow you to wear boots and shoes.”
Because of his delusion and folly, Prince Vigatāśoka slaughtered the Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, some within the city fled toward the west, while others threw themselves into Nepal.
Those who entered Nepāla were all members of the venerable Ānanda’s retinue.
Later, some merchants from Śrāvastī, carrying various goods, headed toward Nepāla. Upon seeing these merchants, the Śākyas asked:
"We are now beset by such hardship and distress; will the noble Ānanda not come here to visit us?"

At that time, the merchants remained single-mindedly mindful; once their trade was concluded, they returned to the city of Śrāvastī and reported in detail to the noble Ānanda that his kinsmen were in Nepāla, speaking as follows.
When the noble Ānanda heard these words from the merchants, his heart was filled with sorrow, and he immediately departed for the kingdom of Nepāla.
The country was extremely cold and snowy; Ānanda’s hands and feet were cracked and split, so he returned to Śrāvastī.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked, "Ānanda!
Previously your hands and feet were as soft as a tongue; why are they now so cracked and split?"
He replied, “I am from the kingdom of Nepāla, a land near the Snow Mountains.
It is because of the wind and snow that my hands and feet have become like this.”
He asked again,
"How do your followers survive there? He replied:
"He is wearing leather boots.
He asked again,
"Why do you not wear them?"
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted its use.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In places where there is cold snow, one should wear *puṭa* boots.
Then the Venerable Upāli said to the Blessed One:
"As the Buddha has said:"
"In places where there is snow and cold, one should wear *puṭa* (leather footwear).
[The monks asked,] "What is meant by a 'cold and snowy country'?
The Buddha said:
"The water contained in the bowl that has frozen indicates that this is a place of cold snow.
Furthermore, there was a hunter who conceived deep faith in the bhikṣu.
At that time, the hunter obtained a bear skin and offered it to him, but the bhikṣu would not accept it.
The Buddha went there and, knowing the reason, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason is this hunter following after the bhikṣu?
Ānanda then questioned the bhikṣu; having learned the circumstances, he informed the Buddha of the matter, and the Buddha said:

"O rare hunter, you have given rise to pure faith; yet even though a thousand kinds of instruction were given, you ultimately refused to cease the karma of killing. Therefore, we grant you this bear skin."
"Once received, it should be placed beneath the door panel of a Buddha hall, or upon a seat, or at the side of one's feet; it can restore sight to those with impaired vision and cure hemorrhoids.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose leather sandals had worn through the soles. He took them to a cobbler to have them repaired, but when they were not returned after a long time, he went to demand them back.
Another bhikṣu replied,
"Why do you not sew it yourself? He answered:
"Although I am skilled at it, the Blessed One has not yet permitted it.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there are those who are skilled, they should sew their own leather sandals in a private place."
Having received this permission, he went to that bhikṣu’s place and said,
"Venerable one! The Blessed One has already permitted one to sew and patch oneself."
He replied, "I require needles, knives, leather thongs, and so forth. At that time,
the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to keep awls, knives, leather thongs, and thread; there is no offense in any of these.
*The Vinaya on Leather Matters of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, Vol. Lower.
